thread.title: ETFs In Focus: JPMorgan's Underrated Dividend ETF, Betting On India, Investing Tactically In Junk Bonds | Seeking Alpha

author: Dave Dierking, CFA
title: ETFs In Focus: JPMorgan's Underrated Dividend ETF, Betting On India, Investing Tactically In Junk Bonds | Seeking Alpha
text:
Note: The "ETFs in Focus" report gets delivered to ETF Focus subscribers weekly and includes analysis on a number of ETFs that should be on your radar over the coming weeks. Below is a sample of that report. This was first sent to ETF Focus subscribers on November 9. All data is current as of that date.
Let's take a look ahead at the ETFs to watch over the next few weeks!
The Equity ETF Idea I mention dividend ETFs quite a bit here because 1) I believe they deserve a spot in just about every portfolio to some degree and 2) there are a lot of really good options in this space that are worth a mention. A theme that's really been picking up momentum in 2018 is factor ETFs, specifically multi-factor ETFs. One fund that I really like and I think is a bit under the radar is a product that combines the best of three different factors into one.
The O'Shares FTSE US Quality Dividend ETF ( OUSA ) targets companies based on dividend yield, quality and low volatility. The quality factor is based on measures of profitability and leverage, the low volatility factor is determined using the standard deviation of weekly returns and the yield factor looks at the trailing 12-month dividend. Without getting too far into the weeds with the methodology, companies are scored on each of the three factors with the highest combined scores receiving the highest weights in the portfolio.
The focus on these factors predictably gives the portfolio a tilt towards large, mature, cash-rich companies.
What do I like about this fund? The yield of 2.7% is solid if not spectacular, but the historical risk/reward tradeoff over its three-year existence has been really strong. Compared to the average of Morningstar's Large Value category, OUSA has returned about 1.7% more annually with about 20% less risk. Its return per unit of risk was higher than the S&P 500 over that time even though it underperformed the index on an absolute basis. In other words, the fund's strategy works.
On the downside, the expense ratio of 0.48% is a little on the high end, but this is a fund that's ranked in the top 20% of its peer group since inception. Despite the above average fees, I'd give this ETF a well-deserved buy rating.
The Fixed Income ETF Idea One subject that we haven't heard a whole lot about lately in this environment focused on trade, interest rates and earnings is inflation. The Fed often talks about managing to a target 2% inflation rate and, for the most part, inflation has managed to stay right around that level.
The Fed's anticipated path of future rate hikes should likely keep inflation rates in check for now, but what happens if inflation starts ticking up? We've seen that in 2018 where the core inflation started the year below 2% but hit the 2.4% mark just recently. Most people are familiar with Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS. These have an interest rate that's tied to the inflation rate and can increase your income in the event that inflation starts rising. But there's another interesting play out there for rising inflation risk.
The ProShares Inflation Expectations ETF ( RINF ) uses a similar strategy to TIPS but bases its returns not on the actual inflation rate, but the expectations for inflation. The fund uses a long/short strategy that combines a long position in the most recently issued 30-year TIPS and a duration-adjusted short position in U.S. Treasury bonds of approximately the same dollar amount. What you are left with is a fund that rises and falls based just on the future expectations for inflation.
RINF has done quite well this year thanks to the rise in the inflation rate, although the short position in Treasuries no doubt helped its cause.
Because it's a long/short fund, RINF won't be appropriate as a long-term holding, although the short position in Treasuries will likely serve the fund well if interest rates continue to rise. I think this is an interesting alternative fixed income holding during periods of rising rate where most Treasury ETFs could be expected to struggle. The 0.30% expense ratio is fairly reasonable, although like many TIPS ETFs you're not going to get much in the way of yield.
The International ETF Idea If you're looking for an emerging economy to make a long-term investment in, India might be my country of choice. With nearly 1.3 billion residents and an economy that's expected to grow by 7-8% annually over the next five years, it's reasonable to feel optimistic about the country's potential. But like most emerging market nations, Indian equities have struggled this year. The strong dollar coupled with higher energy prices (India is a big importer of oil) have helped to send India ETFs down some 15% this year. Plus, as is the case with many high growth economies, inflation is a concern. India's core inflation rate recently came in around 6%, forcing the Reserve Bank of India to make multiple rate hikes, something that could stifle future growth.
If you're willing to ride out some of the short-term volatility, India looks like a solid long-term opportunity. If you want broad exposure, you could go with a fund, such as the iShares MSCI India Index ETF ( INDA ), by far the biggest India ETF around, but I prefer the WisdomTree India Earnings ETF ( EPI ) instead. It focuses on profitable companies within the country and gives heavier weights to those stocks with greater earnings. Trading at 14 times earnings compared to 20 for INDA, EPI represents a much better value for investors and should help cushion against some of the downside risks should the emerging markets group continue to lag.
The Dividend ETF Idea When you think of big ETF issuers, you may not think of JPMorgan (NYSE: JPM ), but maybe you should. They've climbed from a minimal presence in the ETF industry to the 11 th largest issuer overall. Their BetaBuilders lineup has been a huge success and it looks like they're poised to grow even further.
One of their most underrated offerings comes on the dividend side. The JPMorgan U.S. Dividend ETF ( JDIV ) is just two years old, but it deserves a spot among the elite. The fund starts with the Russell 1000 and then takes a multi-factor approach looking at both yield and volatility. The highest yielding securities within the index are selected with components and sectors getting reweighted in order to diversify risk.
JDIV's expense ratio of 0.12% competes with the cheapest in the space and its 4% yield makes it quite attractive for dividend seekers. With just $28 million in assets, it only ranks #15 in the latest ETF rankings (greater assets tend to lead to lower trading costs, which is a factor in the ranking methodology) but this is a case where you could argue a higher ranking is warranted. JDIV is under the radar right now, but feel comfortable using this ETF as a core dividend holding.
The Smart Beta ETF Idea Factor-tilted ETFs are all the rage right now with multi-factor funds showing particular strength. While it's easy to find ETFs that tilt or weight their portfolios in all different manners, sometimes the simplest strategies still work best.
Equal-weighting is often preferred to traditional market cap-weighting because it helps diversify away concentration risk and makes the ETF less top-heavy. Names such as Apple ( AAPL ) or Microsoft ( MSFT ) tend to be popular, but over time mega-cap stocks tend to underperform mid- and small-caps. Instead of market cap-weighting the S&P 500 and giving 21% of the portfolio's weight to just the top 10 names, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF ( RSP ) gives just a 0.2% allocation to each of the index's components. In RSP, Brighthouse Financial ( BHF ) carries the same weight as Amazon ( AMZN ), Facebook ( FB ) and Bank of America ( BAC ).
RSP is 15 years old and during that time it has outperformed the S&P 500 by roughly 0.7% per year. But because it ends up looking more like a mid-cap ETF than a large-cap ETF, it comes with a bit more risk. Using the standard deviation of returns, RSP has been about 15% riskier than the S&P 500 over its lifetime, although the risk premium has only been about 3% in recent years.
Equal-weighting is the classic case of capturing a higher return in exchange for taking on a bit more risk. If you stick with the S&P 500 (although equal-weight ETFs exist for most market caps and sectors), this strategy can make a lot of sense. You're still mostly in the large-cap arena and giving yourself the opportunity for a noticeably higher return given enough time ( ETFdb.com estimates that RSP still has 2/3 of assets in large-caps).
The Brand New ETF Idea ETF issuers have given us a lot of interesting new products over the past month or so. Among the contenders are the VanEck Vectors Morningstar Global Wide Moat ETF ( GOAT ), a fund that focuses on companies with sustainable competitive advantages, the iShares ESG U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF ( EAGG ), which could end up being one of the largest socially responsible ETFs around and, for you animal lovers, the ProShares Pet Care ETF (PAWZ).
But I want to take a look at the SPDR Kensho Final Frontiers ETF ( XKFF ) . State Street ( STT ) has partnered again with Kensho, a tech firm that specializes in artificial intelligence and machine learning, to target companies whose products and services are driving innovation behind the exploration of the final frontiers, which includes the areas of outer space and the deep sea. I don't know how much money there is to be made in deep sea exploration, but putting people into space on a cheaper and more efficient basis has become a hot topic as people like Elon Musk continue to develop and test their technologies.
Top holdings in this fund include big names, such as Boeing ( BA ), Lockheed Martin ( LMT ) and United Technologies ( UTX ), as well as more specialized companies, such as Aerojet Rocketdyne Holdings ( AJRD ). As is the case with almost all brand new ETFs, it's not worth consideration right now, but I could see this catching on as a more niche portfolio holding over time.
The Bonus ETF Idea Whether or not the high yield bond space looks attractive at this very moment (I still like the SPDR Bloomberg Barclays Short Term High Yield Bond ETF ( SJNK )), this is one of those sectors where it might pay off to have an active manager overseeing the portfolio. The junk bond market can shift rapidly and having a manager that can sift out some of the junk in the space, no pun intended, has the potential to boost returns while helping maintain comparable risk levels.
Such is the case with the First Trust Tactical High Yield ETF ( HYLS ) . It tries to focus on identifying the higher quality, more attractive opportunities in the junk bond space. Like SJNK, it's also leaning towards the short end of the curve in order to protect against rate and credit risk. It also has a small position shorting Treasury bonds, which should provide some help in what should be a rising rate future. The fund is yielding an impressive 5.5%, although the active management comes at a cost. Its 1.10% expense ratio is much higher than the 0.40% number you'll find with SJNK. The question for investors becomes "is the higher cost of active management worth it?" Over HYLS's 5+ year history, the answer so far has been yes.
It's managed to beat the performance of both short- and long-term junk bonds by more than 9% over its life. I generally don't like funds with high expense ratios, but having an active manager overseeing a sector that could experience some choppy waters over the next couple years might not be a bad idea.
